I don't think it's necessary to insert such a fine-grained function into the main flow (Setup). The main flow is expected to be a high-level overview of the major stages (e.g., find, extract, match). Perhaps a better place for this logic would be at the end of matchDeps. This would also eliminate the need for a separate warnIfNoMatches function. For example: ```go func (sp *SetupPhase) matchDeps(...) { .... if len(matched)==0 { .... // print to stderr and log files } return matched, nil } ```

`"GOFLAGS"` is a bare string literal; the rest of this codebase centralizes env var names as constants in `tool/util` (`EnvOtelcWorkDir`, `EnvOtelcBuildFlags`, `EnvOtelcStats`). Not a functional issue since GOFLAGS is a real Go toolchain var rather than an otelc-specific one, just a consistency nit.
Both new tests drive `otelc go build`. Nothing here exercises standalone `otelc setup` against a vendored project. A test on that path would have caught the standalone-command gap noted above.

gosec flags `os.ReadFile(modulesTxt)` here as G304 (potential file inclusion via variable). `modulesTxt` is built from `t.TempDir()` plus a hardcoded literal, not from any external input. Standard test-code false positive, no change needed.

`forceModMod` and `rewriteModVendor` only match single-dash `-mod`/`-mod=vendor`. Go's flag parsing treats `--mod=vendor` / `--mod vendor` as equivalent to the single-dash form, so an invocation using double dashes would skip the rewrite and hit the original vendor-consistency failure. Low real-world odds since single-dash is the near-universal convention, but it's the exact flag this PR exists to neutralize.

`rewriteModVendor` scans positional args without distinguishing flags from build targets. A literal `-mod` token would only be misread if it appeared as some other flag's separate-form value immediately followed by `"vendor"`. Vanishingly unlikely, not worth changing, just noting the tradeoff of positional scanning vs. a flag-aware parser.

Any error from `pkgload.ModuleDir` (missing `go` binary, permission error, context cancellation) is swallowed and treated the same as "not vendored," with no log line. On a real vendored project this fails open into the exact bug the PR fixes, with nothing in the logs pointing at why detection didn't fire.
Lets move these helpers to a separate `vendor.go` file.

`GOFLAGS=-mod=mod` is only forced in `GoBuild` (line 662-670), before `Setup` runs. `otelc setup` is also registered as a standalone CLI command (`tool/cmd/otelc/cmd_setup.go`, `Action: setup.Setup`), and when invoked that way `GoBuild` never runs, so this line's `vendoringActive` result only reaches `findDeps`'s dry run. Nothing forces module mode for `getBuildPackages` at line 318, which runs first and hits the same "inconsistent vendoring" failure this PR fixes. Worth either forcing GOFLAGS at the top of `Setup` too, or documenting that standalone `otelc setup` on a vendored project isn't supported. Neither integration test exercises this path; both go through `otelc go build`.

`vendoringActive` (which shells out to `go env GOMOD`) runs once here and again in `GoBuild` at line 663 for the same directory: two subprocess execs per `otelc go build` invocation. Given the standalone-command gap noted above, the recompute here doesn't currently deliver the coverage it's justified by, so today it's a redundant exec with no corresponding benefit.

`vendoringActive` doesn't check for workspace mode. I confirmed `go env GOMOD` still resolves a workspace member module's real go.mod (not empty/DevNull) even under `go.work`, so a workspace member with a leftover `vendor/modules.txt` makes this return `true`, and `GoBuild` then sets `GOFLAGS=-mod=mod`. Go rejects that outright in workspace mode: `-mod may only be set to readonly or vendor when in workspace mode`. Workspace mode normally ignores per-module vendor directories entirely, so this turns a build that worked before this PR into a hard failure. The "go.work workspaces are out of scope" comment at line 666 isn't backed by an actual `go env GOWORK` guard anywhere in this change.

If the user runs `otelc go build -mod=vendor`, this will still fail. Should we also check whether `restArgs` contains a `-mod` flag and force its value to `mod`? Otherwise the CLI flag takes precedence over `GOFLAGS`, so the top-level `go build` will still use `-mod=vendor`.

Could we reuse `pkgload.ResolveModuleDir` here instead of introducing another way of resolving the module root? We could extend it to first check whether `workDir` is a package directory and use `LoadPackages` to resolve the module directory. If it isn't a package, we could fall back to `go env GOMOD` to locate the active `go.mod`.

`os.Setenv("GOFLAGS", ...)` mutates process-wide env with no restore. Not an issue under the current one-shot-CLI-per-process model, but there's nothing guarding against `GoBuild` running twice in the same process (library embedding, tests that call it repeatedly). If that ever happens, `-mod=mod` from one vendored build leaks into a later non-vendored one.

The vendoring workaround does not account for a `-mod=vendor` flag supplied on the command line (either `-mod=vendor` or `-mod vendor`). Since command-line flags take precedence over `GOFLAGS`, the appended `GOFLAGS=-mod=mod` is ignored for the build, and the modified `go.mod` is still checked against the stale `vendor/modules.txt`, causing the build to fail. The existing build arguments must be inspected before deciding that module mode can be forced.

The vendoring check only inspects `util.GetOtelcWorkDir()`, which is the process working directory and does not account for the effective directory selected by a `-C` build flag. For `otelc go build -C ./submodule` (or when invoked from a parent directory), this can miss `submodule/vendor/modules.txt` and leave the modified `go.mod` in vendor mode, causing the build to fail its vendor consistency check. It can also detect the wrong parent module and force `-mod=mod` for a different target.

The vendoring override only checks `GOFLAGS`, not the command-line build arguments. For a vendored project invoked as `otelc go build -mod=vendor ./...`, this appends `GOFLAGS=-mod=mod`, but the explicit `-mod=vendor` argument takes precedence and Go still performs the stale `vendor/modules.txt` consistency check after setup edits `go.mod`, so the build fails. Detect the `-mod` setting from the parsed build arguments as well (or otherwise handle explicit `-mod=vendor`) before applying this fallback.

This condition does not handle an explicitly requested vendor mode. If `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor`, `goflagsSelectsModMode` returns true and no override is added; if the command contains `-mod=vendor`, the appended `GOFLAGS=-mod=mod` is overridden by the command-line flag. Because setup has modified `go.mod` without updating `vendor/modules.txt`, the subsequent build still runs in vendor mode and fails the vendor consistency check. The explicit `-mod=vendor` case should either be rejected with a clear error or have the vendor metadata updated before building.

`findModuleRoot` cannot detect workspace vendoring. A Go workspace may have `go.work` at the workspace root and `vendor/modules.txt` there, with the build run from one of the workspace modules; this function finds that module’s `go.mod` and only checks `<module>/vendor/modules.txt`. In that valid configuration, the workaround is skipped and the build can fail after setup edits `go.mod` without updating the workspace vendor metadata.

This sets a *local* default, which diverges from how integration does it — `test-integration` / `test-integration/coverage` don't set `OTELC_TEST_GOCACHE` at all; only CI provides it. Consequence: `make test-e2e` on a dev machine now writes one full Go build cache tree **per app** under `test/.otelc-gocache/` (~7 apps across the suite) instead of using the shared `GOCACHE`. That's a nontrivial disk footprint developers don't opt into. Defensible if intentional — local iteration gets warm rebuilds too — but the two suites should probably converge: either add the same default to the integration targets, or keep this CI-only and let the workflow `env:` supply it.

Measured this locally (macOS arm64, `TestGin` only) to put numbers on both sides: **Benefit is real** — cold run 78.0s, warm re-run 21.3s, a 3.7× speedup. This clearly addresses the slow-arm64-runner problem, so no argument with the approach. **Cost is the local default** — one `TestGin` run produced 689 MB under `test/.otelc-gocache/` for just two apps (`ginserver` 405M, `httpclient` 284M). Extrapolated across the ~7 apps the full e2e suite builds, that's roughly 2–2.5 GB appearing on a contributor's disk from a plain `make test-e2e`, separate from their shared `GOCACHE` rather than reusing it. That's the part I'd reconsider: the speedup is what CI needs, but CI already gets it from the `env:` + `actions/cache` step. Keeping the Makefile CI-only (as `test-integration` does) would preserve the win where it matters without changing local disk behaviour. If you'd rather keep the local default, that's defensible — worth a note in `docs/testing.md` so the footprint isn't a surprise, and the integration targets should probably get the same default for consistency.
Is `parallel` necessary? We don't want to make CI slower.

This job sets `OTELC_TEST_GOCACHE` but has no `actions/cache` step, so the per-app cache is built cold and thrown away on every run — none of the cross-run benefit the matrix job below gets. It's not a regression (dropping `-a` still buys within-run reuse, e.g. `httpclient` is built by both `http_test.go` and `gin_test.go`), but as written it looks unintentional. Either add the matching cache step here, or drop this `env:` block. Worth noting the `env:` is a no-op either way: the Makefile default resolves to `$(CURDIR)/test/.otelc-gocache`, and `CURDIR` in CI is already `github.workspace`. The `actions/cache` step is the only part that actually changes behavior.

If `req.OpName` is empty, this emits `"db.operation.name": ""`. Per the [otel AnyValue spec](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/blob/main/specification/common/README.md#anyvalue): > AnyValues expressing an empty value, a numerical value of zero, an empty string, or an empty array are considered meaningful and MUST be stored and passed on to processors / exporters. While it makes sense to always emit `db.query.text` (since an empty query string is literally what was executed), `db.operation.name` represents a category. If no category is available, the attribute should be omitted rather than emitted as `""`.

This formatting (`{keyspace}.{operation}`) doesn't match the [otel db semconv](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.37.0/docs/database/database-spans.md#name). Spec says it should be `{db.operation.name} {target}` (so `"SELECT testks"` instead of `"testks.SELECT"`). If neither `db.operation.name` nor `target` are available, we can fallback to `"cassandra"`.

`ConnectionHost` returns only the Docker host, not the mapped Cassandra port. Since Testcontainers maps port `9042` to a dynamically allocated host port, passing this value to `gocql.NewCluster` makes the client try `host:9042` and the integration test cannot connect. Use the Cassandra module's connection string or append the mapped `9042/tcp` port.

`ConnectionHost` returns only the container hostname, not the host-mapped CQL port. Since Cassandra's exposed port is dynamically mapped by Testcontainers, passing this value to `gocql.NewCluster` makes the client fall back to port `9042` on the host, which will generally fail to connect. Retrieve `ConnectionPort` as well and pass `host:port` (or use the module's connection-string helper).

`FreePort` can call `t.Fatalf`/`require.NoError` (via `FailNow`) from inside this spawned goroutine. Per `testing.T.FailNow` docs: "FailNow must be called from the goroutine running the test... Calling FailNow does not stop those other goroutines." If that path ever fires here, the goroutine `Goexit`s before reaching `ports <- FreePort(t)`. The send never happens, and the receiving loop below blocks on that missing value until the suite's `-timeout` kills it. The real failure (context cancelled, or listen exhausted after 100 attempts) gets replaced by an opaque timeout panic instead of a clear test failure. Low probability under normal CI load, but worth hardening, e.g. run each goroutine as its own `t.Run(..., func(t *testing.T) { t.Parallel(); ... })` subtest so `FailNow` has a valid per-goroutine `*testing.T` to target, instead of sharing the parent `t` across raw goroutines.

On `net.Listen` failure the error is discarded entirely; never logged, never surfaced. On `main`, `require.NoError(t, err)` reported the actual OS error (e.g. "too many open files"). Now, if all 100 attempts fail, the final `t.Fatalf` message is generic ("failed to allocate a unique free port after 100 attempts") with no trace of *why*. A real diagnosability regression versus the previous fail-fast behavior. ```suggestion lis, err := net.Listen("tcp", "localhost:0") if err != nil { t.Logf("FreePort: listen attempt %d/%d failed: %v", i+1, maxAttempts, err) time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond) continue } ```
This is already conflicting after merging #977.

The 30-second expiry can return a port that an earlier caller still owns. `FreePort` has no release mechanism, so a test that obtains a port and takes longer than 30 seconds before binding it can have that port removed from `allocatedPorts`; a concurrent call may then receive the same port and cause nondeterministic bind failures. The registry should remain valid for the lifetime of the reservation, or the API should provide an explicit release tied to the caller's bind lifecycle.

I'd suggest a plain list is enough, no need to spell out a reason for every entry. The {foo.go + foo_test.go} pairing is an easy rule to follow, so there's no real risk of someone dropping a file in as an "escape hatch" out of laziness. In other words, if a file shows up in allowlist.go, that already implies it was a deliberate choice. If the author feels like it, they're welcome to add a one-line comment explaining why, but it shouldn't be required.

The existence check can treat another test file as the production source. For example, `foo_test_test.go` passes when `foo_test.go` exists, even though `foo_test.go` is itself a test file and no `foo_test_test.go` source file exists. Require the expected path to be a non-test `.go` file (and ideally a regular file) so repeated `_test` suffixes are rejected.
